paragraphs: Many woodland wildflowers rely on ants to move their seeds. Each seed carries a small, fat-rich appendage that ants find irresistible, so workers haul the seed back to the nest, eat the appendage, and discard the intact seed in an underground refuse chamber. There the seed is sheltered from rodents and from the fires that periodically sweep the forest floor, and it germinates in soil enriched by the ants' waste. Researchers once assumed that the chief benefit to the plant was distance, since a seed carried far from its parent should face less competition. Measurements, however, show that ants typically move seeds only a few meters. The greater advantage appears to be the safety and fertility of the nest site rather than the distance travelled.
